# sam-projects

**Scope check:** this skill covers **Projects** — the Agent Mesh WebUI feature where a user uploads documents and an assistant answers from them. To control an agent's tone / rules / behavior see `sam-author-agent`; for cloud-managed (Amazon Bedrock) document RAG see `sam-connectors` (knowledge_base); for the `sam config` directory of declarative YAML (also called a "project") see `sam-declarative-config`.

## What a Project is

A **Project** is a document workspace in the WebUI: a user uploads files, Agent Mesh indexes them automatically, and an assistant answers questions grounded in them — **no code, no cloud setup.** It's the primary no-code way to put "a pile of my own documents" behind an assistant.

Projects are a **WebUI + REST feature — there is no `sam` CLI command** for them. The deployment must have **persistence configured** (a database); on a no-persistence dev setup the Projects surface is unavailable. The feature is always on wherever persistence is configured.

## The flow (all in the WebUI)

1. **Projects** → create a project (name + optional description).
2. **Knowledge** section → upload files. Agent Mesh **automatically** builds a search index in the background — wait for the "processing" indicator to finish. Until it does, the assistant can't search those files yet.
3. **Default agent** → pick the agent new chats in the project start with (still switchable per chat).
4. Start a chat **inside the project** and ask. The assistant gets a built-in search over the uploaded files and answers from them.

## What you can upload

Indexed for search: **PDF, Word (`.docx`), PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** (modern Office/OOXML only — **not** legacy `.doc`/`.ppt`, and **not** Excel/`.xlsx`), plus text formats (Markdown, CSV, JSON, XML, YAML, HTML, SVG, plain text, …). Uploads are capped per request by `gateway_max_upload_size_bytes`, **default 50 MB**, raisable by the deployment. (`gateway_artifact_content_limit_bytes`, default 10 MB, is a content threshold for embedding files, not an upload reject.) A **scanned-image PDF with no text layer won't index** — extraction reads an existing text layer, there's no OCR. Other binary types may upload but aren't searched.

## Two project settings — what they do, and their limits

- **The project "Instructions" field DOES steer the assistant — but only as first-message framing.** When a user starts a **new** chat inside the project, Agent Mesh prepends the project's workspace framing plus the Instructions (and description) to the user's first message, so the assistant follows them for tone and framing. Limits worth stating plainly: it is injected as **message context on the first message of a newly started in-project chat** — it is **not** applied as the agent's own system instruction, and it is **not** re-injected into a chat that was already underway. For rules that must hold on every turn, across every agent, put them in the **agent's own instruction** (→ `sam-author-agent`); use the project Instructions field for lightweight, project-scoped guidance.
- **The "default agent" is a convenience default, not a hard binding** — it's the agent new chats in the project open with; the user can change it per chat. Don't describe it as "the project forces this agent."

## "The assistant isn't using my documents" — check, in order

1. **Indexing still running (or never ran).** Uploads index asynchronously — wait for "processing" to finish. If it never starts, the files may all be non-indexable types.
2. **Unsupported / empty-text file.** Scanned-image PDFs, images, or odd binaries yield no searchable text. Re-add as a real PDF / Word / text file.
3. **The chat isn't in the project.** A generic new chat isn't scoped to the project — start the chat from inside the project.
4. **Search is keyword-based (BM25), not semantic.** If the question's wording is very different from the document text, it may not match. Use words closer to what the documents actually say.
5. **No persistence.** Project search needs the deployment's persistence configured; indexing is automatic wherever persistence is present.

Don't invent a tool name (e.g. a `customerdocuments_*` tool seen in the environment) — project search is a single built-in tool named **`index_search`**, auto-added to the agent and surfaced to the model only when the project has a built index. It is a capability over the project's own index, not a separate connector or MCP tool.

## Project vs. knowledge_base connector

Both let an assistant answer from documents — pick by infrastructure, not by feature envy:

| | **Project** | **knowledge_base connector** |
|---|---|---|
| Where docs live | Agent Mesh's own artifact storage | **Amazon Bedrock** (cloud) |
| Indexing | Automatic, local — BM25 keyword | Bedrock-managed vector RAG |
| Setup | Upload in the UI — no cloud | Needs an AWS account + a Bedrock Knowledge Base |
| Best for | No-code, no-cloud, your own files | Teams already on Bedrock / large managed KBs |

**No cloud setup wanted → Project.** Already running a Bedrock Knowledge Base → the `knowledge_base` connector (→ `sam-connectors`).

## Sharing & moving

A project is **owner-private by default**. The owner can share it with teammates as **viewer** (read-only — the project UI offers only the viewer level today; the owner is the project's creator, not a grantable level). A project — its files plus settings (name, description, Instructions, default agent) — can be exported and imported as a ZIP; chat sessions are not included.

# sam-tools-and-skills

This skill covers **custom tools and tool packages** for Agent Mesh agents: Go and Python remote tools that run in the STR (Secure Tool Runtime), inline OpenAPI tools, toolsets, and agent skill bundles. **Scope check:** if a no-code connector type fits (SQL, knowledge base, search, document/graph DBs, REST via OpenAPI shared across agents, remote MCP, Slack, event mesh), use `sam-connectors` first — custom code is for when no connector type fits. Inbound (users/events/MCP clients reaching agents) → `sam-entrypoints`. The agent's instructions/behavior → `sam-author-agent`.

## Picking the construct

| The user wants… | Construct | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Custom logic — **default choice** (compiled binary, typed params, artifacts, zero-network scaffold) | Go remote tool via `pkg/samtoolsdk` | [references/go-tools.md](references/go-tools.md) |
| Custom logic where the user already knows Python or needs a Python-only library | Python remote tool via `sam-tool-sdk` (PyPI) | [references/python-tools.md](references/python-tools.md) |
| One agent calling a REST API from an OpenAPI spec, config-file managed | Inline `tool_type: openapi` tool — but **shared/UI-managed API access is the `api` connector** (`sam-connectors`) | [references/openapi-tools.md](references/openapi-tools.md) |
| A reusable package of always-available tools, uploaded once, attached to many agents | **Toolset** | [references/packaging-and-deploy.md](references/packaging-and-deploy.md) |
| Tools *plus* usage instructions the agent loads on demand (`load_skill`) | **Skill bundle** (SKILL.md + references + optional bundled tools) | [references/packaging-and-deploy.md](references/packaging-and-deploy.md) |

Toolset vs skill in one line: a toolset is bare tools, always on the agent's tool list; a skill is instructions first (progressively disclosed at runtime) with tools optionally bundled. Tools that need workflow guidance → skill; standalone utilities → toolset.

**Prefer Go when the user has no strong preference.** Agent Mesh is a Go product and both languages are first-class, but Go is the smoother default: the scaffold vendors the SDK so builds need no network and no PyPI access, cross-compilation to the deployed STR's arch is built into `sam toolset/skill package`, and a single compiled binary ships with no runtime interpreter or dependency-resolution step. Recommend Go unless the user already works in Python or needs a Python-only library — then Python via `sam-tool-sdk` is fully supported, don't push back.

`sam commands` prints every command and flag of the installed `sam` as JSON. Run it when you want the full CLI surface with all options.

## The intended authoring path (teach this, in order)

1. **Scaffold** — `sam toolset init NAME --lang go|python` or `sam skill init NAME [--with-tool --lang go|python]`. Default to `--lang go` unless the user asked for Python. The scaffold is a *working* tool: compilable code and a `manifest.yaml`, plus `build.sh`/`build.bat` for a **toolset** only — a skill-bundle tool gets no build script, because `validate`/`package` build it for you. Go scaffolds vendor the SDK into `_sdk/samtoolsdk/` from the CLI binary itself — building needs **no network and no access to the Agent Mesh repo**. Python scaffolds depend on `sam-tool-sdk` from PyPI.
2. **Author** — edit the generated tool. Real API names are in the references; do not improvise them.
3. **Validate** — `sam toolset validate` / `sam skill validate` builds for your host and runs the exact `--schema` discovery the STR performs. Run it before every package.
4. **Package & deploy** — `sam toolset package` / `sam skill package` cross-compiles for the deployed STR's architecture and zips for WebUI upload; or keep the source in a declarative-config repo and let `sam config plan` / `apply` build and upload (that flow is owned by `sam-declarative-config`).
5. **Attach** — by name, in the agent builder UI (per-tool config form, secrets masked) or in the agent's declarative spec.

## Hard rules (each counters an observed failure)

- **Go product, Go patterns.** Agent Mesh has **no** `tool_type: python`, no `component_module`/`component_base_path`, no ADK `ToolContext`, no `sam plugin add` — the runtime logs a migration warning for `tool_type: python` and registers nothing. Python tools run as **subprocess remote tools in the STR** via `sam-tool-sdk`. **Never route to `solace-agent-mesh-plugin-creator`** — it is Python Agent Mesh.
- **Scaffold first, never SDK code from memory.** Baseline sessions invented `samtoolsdk.Tool[P]{}`, `tc.LoadArtifact`, `TextResult` — none exist. Start every tool from `sam toolset init` / `sam skill init --with-tool` output and the API tables in the references. If a symbol isn't in the reference, check the scaffold or the SDK source before using it.
- **Remote tools appear as `tool_type: builtin`** on the agent's `tools:` list — the dispatcher falls through to the STR when the name isn't an in-process built-in. Toolset and skill attachment generate these entries for you (`toolsetname__toolname`, `skillname__toolname` — `__` separator, charset `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]`).
- **Two OpenAPI constructs exist — say which and why.** Shared across agents, UI-managed, platform-credentialed → `api` connector (`sam-connectors`). Agent-local, declarative-config-managed → inline `tool_type: openapi`. Recommending an MCP wrapper or a dedicated proxy agent for a plain REST API is wrong when these exist.
- **Never write resource YAML from memory.** Toolset metadata (`kind: toolset`, `spec.config`), agent attachment (`toolsets:`, `toolsetConfigs:`, `skillRefs`), and tool stanzas are authored via the builder UI or the **`sam-declarative-config`** skill (its `toolset.md`, `skill.md`, `tool-build.md`, `agent.md` references are the YAML source of truth). This skill names keys; it does not assemble config blocks. Urgency never licenses memory-YAML.
- **Secrets:** `${VAR}` references, never literals; toolset-level `spec.config` for secrets, per-agent overlay for non-secret tunables. A credential pasted into chat is exposed — say so once, advise rotation, reference it as `${VAR}` thereafter.
- **Cross-compile is part of the product, not the user's problem.** The packaged binary must match the deployed STR's OS/arch; `package` resolves it from the platform (`sam toolset build-target` to inspect; `SAM_TOOL_TARGET_OS`/`SAM_TOOL_TARGET_ARCH` to override). With `--url`, a platform that reports no discovered target stops packaging rather than guessing. **Without `--url`, `--target`, or those env vars, `package` falls back to `linux/arm64`** and only prints a stderr note saying so — so an offline package for any other STR arch must set `SAM_TOOL_TARGET_OS`/`SAM_TOOL_TARGET_ARCH`.

## References

| Topic | File |
|---|---|
| Go tool authoring — verified samtoolsdk API, example, build, sharp edges | [references/go-tools.md](references/go-tools.md) |
| Python tool authoring — sam-tool-sdk patterns, runtime contract, sharp edges | [references/python-tools.md](references/python-tools.md) |
| Inline OpenAPI tools — fields, auth, and the connector-vs-tool discriminator | [references/openapi-tools.md](references/openapi-tools.md) |
| Toolsets & skills — decision, layout, CLI lifecycle, upload, attach, per-agent config | [references/packaging-and-deploy.md](references/packaging-and-deploy.md) |

# sam-troubleshoot

The diagnosis front door for Solace Agent Mesh. When a user reports a **symptom** — "my agent won't respond", "entrypoint 500s", "deploy times out", "a tool failed silently" — work the evidence, don't guess. This is a Go runtime: there is **no `pip`, no community/enterprise edition split, no `sam plugin`, no Python `solace_agent_mesh` package**. Diagnosis is logs + `traceID` correlation + `sam-doctor` + health endpoints + the per-task event log.

## First move: always anchor on `traceID`

Agent Mesh mints one immutable `traceID` (UUIDv7) per user task at the entrypoint, carries it on every broker hop (entrypoint → agent → STR → tools, and across peer delegation), and attaches it to every structured log line. **This is the backbone of every diagnosis.**

1. Turn on JSON logs first so fields are queryable: set `LOG_FORMAT=json` on every component.
2. Grab the failing task's `traceID` from the entrypoint log (or the UI), then follow it everywhere. Match the spelling to the format you turned on in step 1: JSON logs carry it as a field, so filter `jq 'select(.traceID=="<uuid>")'` (or `grep '"traceID":"<uuid>"'`); only text/logfmt output spells it `traceID=<uuid>`. In Datadog Logs use `@traceID:<uuid>`.
3. Identifier slog fields are camelCase: `traceID`, `taskID`, `agentName`, `corrID`/`reqID`, `contextID`, `userID`, `publisherID`. Metric fields are snake_case (`duration_ms`). (`eventSeq`/`publisherId` are A2A wire user-property keys, not log keys — the gap-detector logs the sequence as `lastSeq`/`currentSeq`/`gap`.)

**Silent-failure tell:** if the logs show `event sequence: gap detected on per-publisher stream` (logged at ERROR) or `... duplicate or out-of-order event` (logged at WARN), events were dropped or split mid-stream — usually a broker queue/subscription misconfiguration (e.g. two components sharing a subscription, or duplicate `agent_name`/entrypoint id across pods), not a tool bug. Investigate queue config before the tool.

## The symptom → look-here map

Route by what the user reports. Field detail and commands: [references/diagnose.md](references/diagnose.md).

| Symptom | Most likely causes | First look |
|---|---|---|
| Agent/entrypoint won't start (exits, crashloops) | YAML parse error, missing required key, broker/DB/LLM unreachable at startup, port already bound | startup stderr (`kubectl logs --previous` on crashloop); run `sam-doctor` |
| Agent deployed but won't respond; task hangs | broker connectivity, topic-namespace mismatch between entrypoint and agent, agent never discovered, LLM auth/egress | follow `traceID` from the entrypoint; check broker connect + agent-card discovery |
| Entrypoint returns 500 | downstream error mid-request; persistence write failure | grep the response `errorId` in logs, then its `traceID` for the causal chain |
| Deploy times out | broker not reachable, agent not registering its card, image/secret issues | `sam-doctor`; `kubectl describe pod`; broker connect logs |
| Tool / connector / MCP call fails | STR sandbox error, MCP/OpenAPI auth (401/403), an "SSRF protection" refusal of a private address (the Platform service blocks it unless `SAM_PLATFORM_ALLOW_PRIVATE_MCP` is `true`, a process-wide setting to recommend only when connector users are trusted), dial timeout, tool timeout, toolset stuck `pending`/`failed` | the per-task event log (STIM) + the tool's audit log line; check toolset `discoveryStatus`; for an "SSRF protection" refusal, the Platform service log (link-local and metadata addresses stay blocked even with the opt-out) |
| Requests refused: "…usage budget is used up until <date> UTC…", webhook `429` with `Retry-After` | a spent Agent Mesh budget ("this deployment's usage budget") or user budget ("your usage budget", or a named service account's); "usage budgets can't be checked at the moment" is not a spent budget but an Entrypoint Executor still waiting for the budget state after a restart or month rollover | `sam-operate`'s budgets reference; the **Budgets** page and the user's **Budget** column on **User Management** |
| "Some events are missing" / partial output | per-publisher stream gap (see above) | grep `event sequence` |

## Run `sam-doctor` for connectivity/config preflight

`sam-doctor` validates the environment **before** (or independent of) a running Agent Mesh: broker connectivity + auth, LLM endpoint + key, database reachability + auth, object storage, TLS certificates, OIDC discovery, and (local/wheel only) runtime version + port availability. Run it as a CLI (`sam doctor`) or it runs automatically as the Helm pre-install/pre-upgrade hook. `SAM_DOCTOR_CONTEXT=helm|wheel|local` selects the check set; **unset defaults to `local`** and still runs (a misspelled value is a hard error). Skip individual checks with `SAM_DOCTOR_SKIP_CHECKS=<names>`. Full check list + invocation: [references/diagnose.md](references/diagnose.md).

## Reconstruct a specific task: the task event log (STIM)

When the question is "what exactly did this task do — every LLM call, tool call, artifact op, and where it went wrong", that's the **task event log** (STIM file). It must be enabled, then downloaded per task, then read. Full how-to: [references/task-event-logs.md](references/task-event-logs.md). In short: requires a SQL `session_service` **and** `task_logging.enabled: true` on the entrypoint; download per task via `GET /api/v1/tasks/{taskId}` (a `.stim` file) or it auto-saves under the task output dir on `sam task send`; read the `.stim` YAML directly.

## Hard rules (each counters an observed failure)

- **Never invent diagnostics.** Baselines fabricated kubectl label selectors, health-endpoint paths/ports, env-var names, and doc URLs. Don't. The verified names live in the references; if a name isn't there, say you'd confirm it rather than emit a plausible-looking guess a customer will paste and fail on.
- **`sam-doctor` is the purpose-built preflight — lead with it** for connectivity/config symptoms instead of generic `kubectl`/`curl` flailing.
- **Distinguish the two health surfaces.** The entrypoint's request-path `/health` is a shallow "HTTP listener is up" check (always cheap, not diagnostic). The dedicated workload **health server** exposes `/health` (component health, 503 when unhealthy) and `/ready` (readiness) on a separate port. Point Kubernetes probes at the workload health server, not the shallow one. Ports + override flag: [references/diagnose.md](references/diagnose.md).
- **traceID before tools.** A "tool failed silently" is often a dropped event (`event sequence` gap), not a tool error — confirm the stream is intact before blaming the tool.
- **Deployed-environment logs: filter, don't page.** On a cluster, query your log aggregator on the `traceID` field (every component emits it as a structured field) and scope by namespace and service, rather than paging through raw pod logs one at a time.
- **Distinct from operator config.** "How do I turn on SSO / configure RBAC / rotate a secret / upgrade" is `sam-operate`, not troubleshooting. This skill diagnoses; it doesn't configure.

## References

| Topic | File |
|---|---|
| traceID workflow, slog fields, sam-doctor checks, health endpoints/ports, failure-mode table, per-mode log access | [references/diagnose.md](references/diagnose.md) |
| Task event logs (STIM): enable, locate, download, read, event schema | [references/task-event-logs.md](references/task-event-logs.md) |

The diagnosis front door for Solace Agent Mesh. skills.name: sam-build-apply
skills.desc: Tools the AI Builder agent uses to confirm completion of an Apply Changes flow. Call mark_changes_applied at the end of editing a build to give the FE an explicit signal that the apply has finished — without this, the post-edit "Switch to Test Mode" CTA waits on weaker all-deployed-status heuristics.
skills.body:
---
name: sam-build-apply
description: Tools the AI Builder agent uses to confirm completion of an Apply Changes flow. Call mark_changes_applied at the end of editing a build to give the FE an explicit signal that the apply has finished — without this, the post-edit "Switch to Test Mode" CTA waits on weaker all-deployed-status heuristics.
tags:
  - builder
  - apply
---

# Build Apply Skill

You are loaded by the AI Builder agent. Your job is to provide a single
explicit completion marker the frontend can detect when an Apply Changes
flow finishes.

## When to call `sam-build-apply__mark_changes_applied`

Call this tool **once**, at the very end of a flow where:

1. The user previously clicked **Apply Changes** in Test mode, and
2. You (the build agent) received the recommendations message and edited
   one or more components in response, and
3. Every component you modified has been redeployed and is back in a
   working state.

The frontend uses the artifact this tool writes to:
- swap the canvas component pills back to "Active" with confidence the
  edits are settled,
- render the post-edit "Changes are completed!" summary inline in chat,
- show the "Go to Test Mode" CTA so the user can immediately re-test
  the changes.

If you call it before the redeploy finishes, the FE will surface the
completion UI prematurely — wait until validation + deploy succeed.

If you don't call it at all, the FE falls back to the same heuristic
it used before this skill existed (every session-origin component is
deployed) — usable but slower / less reliable.

## Tool

### `sam-build-apply__mark_changes_applied`

Records the apply outcome in a structured `apply_complete.json` artifact
in the current chat session. Parameters:

```json
{
  "summary": "<one-paragraph natural-language summary of what changed>",
  "changesApplied": [
    {
      "component": "<component name>",
      "area": "system_prompt" | "tools" | "workflow_logic" | "model_choice" | "other",
      "change": "<concrete description of the edit>"
    }
  ]
}
```

`summary` becomes the chat-visible "Changes are completed! Here is the
summary:" body. `changesApplied` is rendered as a per-component list
with priority-style colour coding so the user can scan what moved.

    tool_name: redirect_user

# Redirect to Builder

`redirect_user` sends the user to the **Solace Agent Mesh Builder**, which creates agents, workflows, entrypoints and connectors.

Call it as soon as the user wants to create or set up one of those, turn something from this conversation into a reusable agent or automation, or automate a process they do by hand:

1. Say in one sentence what they want to build.
2. Call `redirect_user` with `context`: what they want and why, plus any requirements, tools, data sources or integrations they mentioned. Put the names of relevant uploaded files in `artifacts` so they carry over.

The user then sees a button that opens the Builder with that context and those files.

Never build, design or plan the component yourself. Don't write YAML, agent instructions, workflow definitions or tool definitions, don't ask clarifying questions first, don't ask for uploads, and don't delegate the build to a peer agent. The Builder does all of that.

## Outside the web UI

When the system prompt has an **"Entrypoint Redirect Capability"** note saying redirect buttons can't be rendered (Slack, Teams, MCP, REST), no button appears. Reply in one short message that building Agent Mesh components is only available in the Builder in the Agent Mesh web UI. You may call the tool once, but don't describe a destination page, don't retry, and never build the component yourself.

skills.body:
---
name: sam-docx
description: Create Word (.docx) documents. Provides sam-docx__docx_create_document — build a document from an ordered list of content blocks (headings, paragraphs with inline formatting, bullet/numbered lists, tables, images, page breaks, a real Word table-of-contents field). Load this skill for any "write this up as a Word doc" / report / memo task.
tags:
  - word
  - docx
  - document
  - report
  - office
---

# Word Document Skill

You create Word (`.docx`) documents with **`sam-docx__docx_create_document`**. It
builds a document from a **content-spec artifact**: a YAML or JSON array of
blocks, applied in order.

There is no read/edit tool here — for extracting or reasoning over an
*existing* `.docx`, use `convert_file_to_markdown` instead. This tool only
creates new documents.

## Workflow

1. **Save the content spec as an artifact.** Use the
   `«««save_artifact: filename="doc-spec.yaml" mime_type="application/yaml" tags="__working" description="..."»»»`
   fenced block. Tag it `__working` — it's an
   intermediate, not the deliverable.
2. **Call `docx_create_document`** with `content` set to that filename (and
   `title`, optionally `author`/`subject`/`output_name`/`images`).

Artifact-first, same reasoning as the pptx tool: documents rarely come out
right on the first pass, and editing the spec in place with
`artifact_search_and_replace_regex` is cheaper than re-emitting the whole
block array every revision.

## Block Types

| Type | Fields |
|---|---|
| `heading` | `level` (1-4, required), `text` (required) |
| `paragraph` | `text`, or `runs[]` for mixed formatting in one line; `align` |
| `bullet_list` | `items[]` |
| `numbered_list` | `items[]` |
| `table` | `headers[]`, `rows[][]`, `header_bold` (default true), `col_widths[]` (default: even split) |
| `image` | `image_ref` (required; quoted index into top-level `images[]`), `width_in` (default 4), `height_in` (default: preserves aspect ratio), `align` |
| `page_break` | *(no fields)* |
| `table_of_contents` | `toc_title` (default "Table of Contents"; `""` for no heading), `toc_levels` (default "1-3") |

Each block reads **only** the fields listed for its own type, and the same
applies to the fields inside a `runs` entry. A field on the wrong type, or
misspelled, is rejected rather than ignored — so a `heading` carrying `runs` is
an error, not an empty heading, and a `txt:` typo inside a run is an error
rather than a silently dropped span. Key names are matched case-insensitively.
Every problem in the spec is reported at once, so one revision fixes the whole
array.

`align` is `left` \| `center` \| `right` \| `justify` (paragraph and image
blocks); case and spacing don't matter, anything else is an error. A `runs`
entry is `{text, bold?, italic?, underline?, color?}` — `color` accepts
`C0392B`, `#C0392B`, or the `#abc` shorthand, but a colour *name* like `red` is
an error rather than a silent fallback to black.

`toc_levels` is a single digit or a hyphenated range (`"1-3"`); a comma-separated
list is an error. Note the default `"1-3"` omits level-4 headings.

Rows shorter than the widest row are padded. A table is limited to 63 columns
(Word's own maximum) — hitting that almost always means one row was written as a
flat list of every value instead of being nested as its own row.

Every table spans the full page width. With no `col_widths` the columns split
that width evenly, and readers are free to narrow a column to fit its content —

columns hold comparable amounts of text.

long prose: an even split gives the labels far more room than they need and
wraps the prose column hard. A "Principle | Description" table reads better as

that disagrees with the table's column count is an error rather than a guess.

1/10 inch, so `[1, 10000]` gives a narrow first column rather than one collapsed
to nothing — a collapsed column clips its content instead of wrapping it.

```yaml
  text: "1. Highlights"
- type: bullet_list

- type: paragraph

    - text: "99.94%"
      bold: true
    - text: " over the rolling 30-day window."
- type: heading
  level: 1
  text: "2. Metrics"
- type: table
  headers: ["Metric", "Q2", "Q3"]
```

creates new documents.

skills.desc: Read, create, and modify Excel (.xlsx) workbooks. Provides sam-excel__xlsx_read (selective, context-safe reading — describe / range / row-window / cell-search) and sam-excel__xlsx_write (create or modify via an ordered list of openpyxl-style operations — set cells, fill ranges directly from CSV/JSON data artifacts, stamp formulas across whole ranges, style, merge, freeze panes, auto-filter, charts). Load this skill for any spreadsheet task.
skills.body:
---
name: sam-excel
description: Read, create, and modify Excel (.xlsx) workbooks. Provides sam-excel__xlsx_read (selective, context-safe reading — describe / range / row-window / cell-search) and sam-excel__xlsx_write (create or modify via an ordered list of openpyxl-style operations — set cells, fill ranges directly from CSV/JSON data artifacts, stamp formulas across whole ranges, style, merge, freeze panes, auto-filter, charts). Load this skill for any spreadsheet task.
tags:
  - excel
  - xlsx
  - spreadsheet
  - data
  - office
---

# Excel Skill

You work with Excel (`.xlsx`) workbooks. Two tools are bundled here:

- **`sam-excel__xlsx_read`** — read a workbook *selectively*: orient with `describe`, then pull only the range/rows you need, read formulas, or search for cells. Never dumps a whole workbook into context.
- **`sam-excel__xlsx_write`** — create a new workbook or modify an existing one by applying an ordered list of **openpyxl-style operations**.

The vocabulary mirrors **openpyxl + native Excel**: A1 notation everywhere (`A1`, `C2:C100`, `Sheet1!$A$2:$A$50`), real Excel formulas (`=SUM(B2:B40)`), and openpyxl-style styling (font, fill, alignment, number format). Use them the way you'd use openpyxl.

Two habits matter most:

1. **Fill from data artifacts — don't re-type data.** When the rows already exist as a CSV/JSON artifact (e.g. produced by another tool or a template render), use the `fill_from_data` operation to stamp them into a sheet. Do **not** read the data in and re-emit it as inline `values`.
2. **Read selectively.** Always `describe` first, then read a bounded `range` / `rows` window or `search` for what you need. A whole-sheet read over the cell cap returns guidance to narrow, not the data.

---

## Reading: `sam-excel__xlsx_read`

Start every read task with `describe`:

```json
{ "source": "report.xlsx", "mode": "describe" }
```

It returns, per sheet: dimensions, row/column counts, the header row, merged ranges, and defined names. Then pull only what you need:

- **A bounded block** — `{ "source": "report.xlsx", "mode": "values", "sheet": "Q3", "range": "A1:E25" }`
- **A row window** — `{ "source": "report.xlsx", "mode": "values", "rows": "1-50" }`
- **Find a cell without reading the sheet** — `{ "source": "report.xlsx", "mode": "search", "query": "Total Revenue" }` (set `"regex": true` for patterns)
- **Inspect formulas** — `{ "source": "report.xlsx", "mode": "formulas", "sheet": "Q3", "range": "F2:F40" }`

`format` controls rendering: `markdown` (default), `csv`, or `json_rows`. Whole-sheet `values` reads above `max_cells` (default 2000) return the sheet size and tell you to narrow — respond by scoping with `range`/`rows` or using `search`.

See `references/reading.md` for the full selective-read playbook.

---

## Writing: `sam-excel__xlsx_write`

Omit `source` to **create** a new workbook; pass an existing `.xlsx` artifact as `source` to **modify** it. Operations apply in order; the whole call produces **one** new artifact version at the end (not one per operation).

**Versioning & `output_name`:** when modifying, leave `output_name` unset — it defaults to the `source` filename, so the edit saves as the next version of the same workbook (artifacts are immutable and versioned; the prior version stays addressable as `name.xlsx:1`). Set `output_name` only when you want to fork a separate, differently-named copy. A fresh create with no `output_name` saves as `workbook.xlsx`.

### Filling a sheet from a data artifact (the common case)

When the data already lives in a CSV/JSON artifact, reference it in `data_sources` and stamp it with `fill_from_data` — no manual re-entry:

```json
{
  "output_name": "q3-sales",
  "data_sources": ["sales_rows.csv"],
  "operations": [
    { "op": "rename_sheet", "sheet": "Sheet1", "new_name": "Q3" },
    { "op": "fill_from_data", "sheet": "Q3", "anchor": "A1", "source": "0", "include_header": true },
    { "op": "set_cell", "sheet": "Q3", "cell": "D1", "value": "Margin" },
    { "op": "set_formula_range", "sheet": "Q3", "range": "D2:D41", "formula": "=C2/B2" },
    { "op": "set_cell", "sheet": "Q3", "cell": "B42", "formula": "=SUM(B2:B41)" },
    { "op": "set_style", "sheet": "Q3", "range": "A1:D1",
      "style": { "bold": true, "font_color": "FFFFFF", "fill": "4472C4" } },
    { "op": "set_style", "sheet": "Q3", "range": "D2:D41", "style": { "number_format": "0.0%" } },
    { "op": "freeze_panes", "sheet": "Q3", "cell": "A2" },
    { "op": "auto_filter", "sheet": "Q3", "range": "A1:D41" }
  ]
}
```

### Stamping formulas across a range

`set_formula_range` fills a formula across a whole range in one op — never write a column of formulas cell by cell. The default `shared` mode auto-adjusts relative references per cell (`=A2*B2` → `=A3*B3` …) while preserving absolute refs and quoted sheet names. Use `mode: "template"` with `{row}`/`{col}` tokens only when relative adjustment doesn't fit.

### Modifying an existing workbook

```json
{
  "source": "budget.xlsx",
  "operations": [
    { "op": "set_cell", "sheet": "FY26", "cell": "C7", "value": 125000 },
    { "op": "set_style", "sheet": "FY26", "range": "C7", "style": { "number_format": "$#,##0" } }
  ]
}
```

### Operation catalog (summary)

| Group | Operations |
|---|---|
| Structure | `create_sheet`, `delete_sheet`, `rename_sheet` |
| Data | `set_cell`, `set_values`, `fill_from_data` |
| Formulas | `set_formula_range` |
| Styling | `set_style`, `merge`, `unmerge` |
| Layout | `set_col_width`, `set_row_height`, `freeze_panes`, `auto_filter` |
| Advanced | `add_chart`, `set_defined_name` |

Full per-operation field reference and the complete `style` object (font, fill, border, alignment, number formats) are in `references/operations.md`. More worked examples (charts, multi-sheet, formatting recipes) are in `references/examples.md`.

### Inline operations vs an operations artifact

- **Inline `operations`** — use for small, targeted edits (a handful of ops). Most modify tasks.
- **`operations_artifact`** — for large or iterative builds, save the operations array as a YAML/JSON artifact and pass its filename. You can then edit it in place with `artifact_search_and_replace_regex` and re-run, rather than re-emitting the whole list. When set, it takes precedence over inline `operations`.

---

## Guidance

- **Numbers stay numbers.** Pass numeric cell values as JSON numbers (`125000`, not `"125000"`) so they're real numbers in the sheet. `fill_from_data` coerces clean numeric CSV cells automatically.
- **Format numbers with `number_format`, not by pre-rounding.** Apply `0.0%`, `$#,##0`, `#,##0.00`, `yyyy-mm-dd` etc. via `set_style` so the underlying value stays precise.
- **One header, then freeze it.** After a header row, `freeze_panes` at the cell below-left (e.g. `A2`) and add `auto_filter` over the data range for anything tabular.
- **Iterate cheaply.** To revise a generated workbook, modify the source artifact with targeted ops rather than regenerating from scratch.

## References

- `references/operations.md` — every operation, field by field, plus the full style object and number-format / color / border reference.
- `references/examples.md` — worked examples: charts, multi-sheet workbooks, JSON-object fills, formatting recipes.
- `references/reading.md` — the selective-read playbook (describe → narrow → search) and context-safety rules.

description: Comprehensive knowledge about Solace Agent Mesh — what it is, how it works, worker examples, and FAQs.

  - onboarding

# Solace Agent Mesh: Your AI Workforce Manager

## What Is Solace Agent Mesh?

Solace Agent Mesh is an AI workforce manager. It lets you create digital workers, assign them roles, give them the tools and credentials they need, and put them to work. These workers are always available — ready to react to events the moment they happen, execute tasks on schedule, and collaborate with each other to get complex jobs done. They don't sit idle burning resources; they spring into action when there's work to do.

Think of Solace Agent Mesh the way you'd think about managing a team. You don't write code to handle every situation yourself. Instead, you define what needs to happen, hire the right people, and let them do their jobs. Agent Mesh works the same way: you describe the work, and Agent Mesh builds and manages the digital workers to carry it out.

Each worker in Solace Agent Mesh is a self-contained unit with a clear responsibility. It has its own agents (the AI brains that make decisions), workflows (the structured processes that coordinate multi-step work), task schedules (when things should happen), and credentials (the keys and tokens needed to interact with external systems). More technical users can dive deeper — configuring agents directly, writing custom tools, designing complex workflows — but the conversational interface is the primary way most people interact with Agent Mesh.

**What AI models does Solace Agent Mesh use?**
Agent Mesh works with all major AI providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, and others. You choose which model powers your workers based on your preferences for capability, cost, and data privacy. Agent Mesh also supports local models for organizations that need to keep everything on-premises.

**Is my data secure?**
Solace Agent Mesh runs on your infrastructure — your machine, your cloud, your data center. Your data doesn't pass through any third-party systems except the AI model provider you choose. Credentials are stored locally with encryption. Enterprise deployments add RBAC, audit logging, and trust management for organizational security requirements.

**Can workers make mistakes?**
Yes, just like human workers can. Solace Agent Mesh provides several safety mechanisms: human-in-the-loop approval for sensitive actions (before a worker deploys code or sends an email to a customer, it can ask for your confirmation), audit trails of everything workers do, and configurable guardrails that limit what actions workers can take autonomously. You decide the trust level for each worker.

**How does Solace Agent Mesh handle work that spans multiple systems?**
This is where Agent Mesh shines. Because workers communicate through the event mesh, a single business process can span any number of systems transparently. A customer complaint might involve the support system, the billing platform, the product backlog, and the customer success tool — Agent Mesh workers coordinate across all of them without you having to build point-to-point integrations.

**Can I use Solace Agent Mesh for my team, not just myself?**
Yes. Agent Mesh Enterprise adds multi-user support with role-based access control, shared workers that serve an entire team, and centralized management of the digital workforce. Individual team members can interact with workers through chat, while administrators manage worker configurations, credentials, and permissions.

# Solace Agent Mesh Observability Reference

This skill is the reference the admin observability agent uses to interpret the
data its tools return. It explains the data model, what the numbers mean, how to
judge health, and how to read failures.

## The data model

- **Task** — a unit of work submitted into the mesh (via an entrypoint or a
  scheduled task). Has an id, owning `userId`, `status`, `startDate`/`endDate`,
  token usage, and an `executionMode` (`foreground` or `background`). A task's
  `kind` is normally `task`; rows with `kind=compaction-cost` are internal
  accounting and are excluded from the health/usage reports.
- **Status** — terminal: `completed` (success), `failed` / `error` / `timeout`
  (counted as failures), `cancelled` (user-initiated stop, NOT a failure).
  Non-terminal: `running`, `pending`. A NULL status shows as `unknown`.
- **Agent** — a deployed worker addressable over A2A. A task is routed to a
  target agent via a `…/agent/request/<agentName>` broker topic; that topic is
  how per-agent attribution is derived (best-effort).
- **Gateway** — the ingress that submits tasks and owns the operational store
  (tasks, task events, feedback, scheduled tasks).
- **Scheduled task** — a cron/interval definition that fires executions against
  a target agent; each run is a `ScheduledTaskExecution` with its own status.
- **Feedback** — a per-task user rating (e.g. `up`/`down`) with an optional
  comment.

A single task threads one `traceID` through every hop — use
`correlate_task_with_logs` to pull exactly the log lines emitted during a task.

## What the numbers mean

- **successRate / errorRate** — fractions of all tasks in the window.
  successRate = `completed / total`; errorRate = `(failed+error+timeout)/total`.
  Always state the denominator and window — a 50% error rate over 4 tasks is
  noise; over 4,000 it is an incident.
- **avgDurationMs / p50 / p95** — computed over *completed* tasks only (tasks
  with an end time). p95 is the latency the slowest 5% experience; watch it more
  than the average, which hides tails.
- **activeBackgroundCount** — background tasks still running (no end time),
  independent of the window. A steadily climbing value suggests stuck tasks.
- **Token usage** — input/output/cached token sums per day or per user. This is
  usage, not cost. **Cost is not in the task store** — it lives in the OTel
  `gen_ai.cost.total` metric (Prometheus / Datadog). For spend, report tokens
  and point the operator at the metrics dashboards rather than estimating.
- **Agent performance** — invocationCount, errorCount, successRate, avg/p95 per
  agent. Attribution is best-effort from routing events; tool-level metrics are
  not here (they live in the OTel `operation.duration` metric).
- **Scheduled-task health** — enabled vs disabled counts, execution outcomes by
  status, and currently-failing tasks (non-zero `consecutiveFailureCount`) with
  their last error. A rising consecutive-failure count is the early warning.

## How to read health

Scan with the status emoji and these rough bands (tune to the deployment's
baseline — compare a window against the prior equivalent period):

- ✅ healthy — errorRate near baseline, p95 within normal range, no climbing
  background count, no scheduled tasks failing repeatedly.
- ⚠️ degraded — errorRate or p95 elevated vs baseline, a few new failures, a
  scheduled task with 1–2 consecutive failures.
- ❌ failing — a specific agent/task class erroring, or a scheduled task failing
  every run.
- 🚨 critical — broad error spike, p95 multiples of baseline, or many tasks
  stuck (activeBackgroundCount climbing without completion).

## Common failure modes

| Mode | How it shows up | How to confirm |
|---|---|---|
| LLM/provider error (rate limit, timeout) | `error`/`timeout` status, bursty | Datadog logs for the agent around the task time; provider 429/5xx |
| Tool error | task `error` after a tool step | `correlate_task_with_logs` on the traceID; look for the tool's error line |
| Config error | consistent failure for one agent right after a deploy | per-agent errorRate spike from a point in time; deploy correlation |
| A2A delegation failure | orchestrator/coordinator tasks fail mid-plan | logs showing a peer request with no response |
| User/input error | isolated failures, varied agents | request text shows malformed/unsupported input |
| Transient infra | brief spike that recovers on its own | error window bounded; no code/deploy change |

## Datadog query patterns

- The Datadog tools automatically scope queries to this deployment's
  `cluster_name` and `kube_namespace` — you only supply the query body.
- Error sweep: `datadog_get_errors` (optionally `service: gateway` / `awe`).
- Task correlation: `correlate_task_with_logs` with the task's `traceID` (it
  builds `@traceID:<id>`). Widen the window for older tasks.
- Free-form: `datadog_query_logs` with a Datadog query like
  `status:error service:awe @agentName:search-agent`.
- Cross-reference the `using-datadog` knowledge for the deployment's exact
  service/namespace names and how slog fields are parsed.

# PowerPoint Deck Skill

You build decks with **`pptx_create_presentation`** from Document Tools. Its own
instructions list every layout and field; this skill is about the judgment around
it: what to put in the deck, how to get there without running out of model calls,
and how to check the result.

## Workflow

1. **Plan the story first.** Decide the 5–8 slides before gathering anything: a
   title, the headline result, one slide per question the user asked, and a
   closing takeaway. Each slide makes one point; its title states that point
   ("Electronics led revenue at $15.7M"), not just the topic ("Revenue").
2. **Gather the figures in as few calls as possible.** The task has a limited
   number of model calls (30 by default), and the deck is the last step, so data
   gathering must leave calls in hand.
   - Compute each slide's figures in one query, or several slides' figures in
     one query, with common table expressions, window functions, or a
     `UNION ALL` of labelled rows. A dozen metrics is three or four queries.
   - Make independent tool calls in the same response.
   - Don't render chart images: the deck draws its own charts (below).
3. **Save the slide spec as one compact artifact.** Use a
   `«««save_artifact: filename="deck-spec.yaml" mime_type="application/yaml" tags="__working" description="..."»»»`
   block, tagged `__working` because it is an intermediate. The whole spec is
   written in one response, so keep it small: round figures (`$15.7M`, not
   `$15,712,384.27`), at most 8 table rows, at most 12 chart categories, and short
   bullets. A spec cut off by the output limit produces no deck at all.
4. **Call `pptx_create_presentation`** with `slides` set to that filename and a
   `title`. Pass image artifacts in `images`, and reference each from an image
   layout slide with `image_ref`.
5. **Check it once.** Skip this for a simple deck, or when few calls remain.
   Otherwise, if `render_document_to_images` is available, render the deck
   (its `pages` option limits which pages), load the page images with
   `load_artifact`, and look for overflowing text, medallions with only a letter
   or the wrong glyph, unreadable charts and repeated layouts. Fix the spec artifact in place (with
   `artifact_search_and_replace_regex` if you have it) and rebuild, once. Don't
   iterate on cosmetics.
6. **Reply briefly.** Give the deck and two or three sentences on what it shows.
   Don't repeat the whole deck in chat.

## Choosing layouts

Vary the layouts. A deck of ten `bullet_list` slides reads as a document. Match
the layout to the kind of point:

| The point is… | Use |
|---|---|
| One headline number | `big_number` (`big_number: "$32.2M"`, `big_label`, short `body`) |
| A trend over time | `chart` with `chart_type: line` (or `area`) |
| A ranking or comparison across categories | `chart` with `chart_type: bar` |
| Shares of a whole (up to about six parts) | `chart` with `chart_type: pie` or `doughnut` |
| Exact figures someone will read across | `table` (at most 8 rows; put "Other" last if you cut) |
| Two things side by side | `comparison` |
| A few findings or recommendations | `icon_grid` or `bullet_list` |
| One thing that stands out | `callout`: the lead-in in `title` (the tool highlights it), the sentence in `body` |
| Phases or next steps | `timeline` or `process` |

Set an `icon` on every `icon_grid`, `timeline` and `process` item and every
`callout`. Without one, an item gets a glyph guessed from its words or just a
letter, and a callout gets no icon at all.

## Charts and tables

Charts are native PowerPoint charts: the viewer can restyle them and read the
values, and they cost nothing extra to make. Put the numbers straight into
`chart_data`:

```yaml
- layout: chart
  title: "Revenue peaked in November"
  chart_data:
    chart_type: line
    show_legend: false
    series:
      - name: "Net revenue ($K)"
        categories: ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
        values: [1910, 2050, 2380, 2440, 2510, 2490, 2560, 2620, 2700, 2930, 3610, 3790]
```

- Use one unit per chart and say it in the series name ("Net revenue ($K)",
  "Orders (units)", "Margin (%)").
- Several series share one set of categories; give each a `name`.
- Sort bar categories by value unless the order means something (months, sizes).
- A table's cells are strings: format them (`"$1.36M"`, `"8.1%"`) before writing.

## Brands

Two things shape a deck's look, and they control different parts:

- **The template profile** decides the slide backgrounds, title and body
  colours, any logo and decorations, and the footer. The agent's tool
  configuration names it (`template_profile`).
- **The `theme` parameter** recolours what the profile leaves open: the heading
  and body fonts, and the accent colours used by charts and cards.

When the user asks for a brand and a loaded skill defines it (colours, fonts, a
logo), pass its fonts and colours as `theme`, and don't invent brand colours.
Otherwise leave `theme` out. `theme` does not
change slide backgrounds or a profile's logo, so tell the user if the result
doesn't look like the brand. To show the brand's logo, put it in `images` and
use an `image_center`, `image_left` or `image_right` slide with `image_ref`; the
`title` layout cannot place one. Don't set `style` unless the user asks for a
particular look.

## Common failures

- **Running out of calls before the deck.** One query per metric, or a chart
  image per figure, spends the budget on gathering. Batch queries and use native
  charts.
- **A spec too large to write in one response.** Raw unrounded figures, long
  tables and paragraph bullets. Round, cut, and summarize.
- **Every slide the same layout.** See the table above.
- **Titles that name a topic instead of making a point.**

# Python Code Execution Skill

You have access to an **`execute_python_code`** tool that runs Python you generate
inside the Secure Tool Runtime sandbox. It is general-purpose: use it for **any**
computation that's easier to express as code — calculations, algorithms, data generation,
data wrangling/analysis, statistics, simulations, format conversion, and chart/file
generation. Reading existing artifacts is just one optional capability, not a requirement;
plenty of useful runs take no input artifacts at all.

## How It Works

1. Pass your Python source as the `python_code` parameter. That alone is enough for
   self-contained work (e.g. compute something, generate data with `faker`, solve with
   `sympy`, build a chart or spreadsheet from scratch).
2. **Only if your code reads an existing artifact**, list its filename in the
   `input_artifacts` argument (e.g. `input_artifacts=["sales.csv"]`) and access it via
   `INPUT_ARTIFACTS["sales.csv"]`. Omit `input_artifacts` entirely when you don't read
   any. (As a safety net the runtime also auto-detects names your code references via
   `INPUT_ARTIFACTS[...]` and loads ones that exist in the session, but declaring them is
   clearest.)
3. Your code computes, produces output files with `save_artifact(...)` or by writing them
   directly in its working directory (e.g. `df.to_csv("top.csv")`), and `print(...)`s
   anything it wants returned as text.
4. The tool returns captured stdout as the result and registers the output files as
   artifacts on the task, so the agent (and later tool calls) can reference them.

## Runtime contract — globals available to your code

<!-- Maintainers: keep the artifact accessor list below (especially the .as_file()
     guidance) in sync with the execute_python_code docstring in
     tools/python/python_executor/python_executor.py. Both reach the model. -->

- **`INPUT_ARTIFACTS`** — a `dict` keyed by artifact filename. Each value exposes:

# Redirect to Scheduled Tasks

You now have access to the `scheduled_task_redirect` tool, which sends the user to the **Scheduled Tasks** page. Scheduled tasks are Solace Agent Mesh tasks that run automatically on a schedule (cron, interval, or one-time) — for example, *"send me a market summary every Monday at 9am"*.

The destination page renders a **preview panel** (next run times, agent target, message body) and lets the user manually edit any field before saving. Because the user always reviews and confirms on the destination page, you do NOT need to gather every detail or ask for confirmation in chat — your job is to recognize the intent and redirect promptly.

## Modes

The tool's `mode` argument picks the destination experience:

| Mode | When to use | Required args |
|------|-------------|---------------|
| `create` | User wants to schedule something new | `context` |
| `view` | User wants to see what's currently scheduled | `context` |
| `edit` | User wants to change an existing task | `context`, `task_id` |
| `delete` | User wants to remove an existing task | `context`, `task_id` |

For `edit` and `delete`, `task_id` is the existing scheduled task's ID. If you don't know it (the user named the task informally and there's no `task_id` in conversation), use `mode=view` so the user can pick the task themselves on the destination page — do NOT guess.

## How to Use This Tool

**Act quickly.** Write a brief preview message (described below), then call `scheduled_task_redirect` immediately. No multi-turn back-and-forth, no clarifying questions.

1. Recognize scheduling intent: words like *every Monday, every morning, weekly, daily, at 9am, on the 1st, recurring, schedule, remind me, run automatically, in two hours, tomorrow at...* — anything that says "run this later or on a schedule".
2. Pick the mode (create / view / edit / delete).
3. **Write the preview message** (see "Preview Message Pattern" below) — this prepares the user for the destination page.
4. Call the tool with:
   - **`context`** (required): a one-to-two sentence summary of what the user wants. Echo only what the user actually said — do NOT invent times, days, frequencies, or other scheduling details they did not provide. For `create` this becomes the prompt pre-filled into the destination AI builder (*"Schedule a market summary report. The user mentioned Monday mornings."*). For `edit` describe the change (*"Move the run time from Monday to Tuesday."*). For `delete` name the task. For `view` a short framing line is enough.
   - **`mode`** (required): one of `create`, `view`, `edit`, `delete`.
   - **`task_id`** (required for `edit` and `delete`): the scheduled task's ID.
   - **`artifacts`** (optional): filenames uploaded in this conversation that are relevant to the scheduled task; they will be copied to the destination session.
5. The user sees the preview message followed by a button that navigates to the Scheduled Tasks page with context pre-loaded.

## Preview Message Pattern

Before calling the tool, write a single short message that **names the Scheduled Tasks page up front** and lists what the user will be able to do there. The page name MUST appear before you describe what the user can do, otherwise "you'll be able to..." is hanging.

**Template:**

```
I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can:

- Review and adjust the schedule{{ if user-mentioned-timing }} ({{user-mentioned-timing}}){{ end }}
- Customize {{what-the-task-does (paraphrasing what the user said)}}
- See a preview of when the task will run
- Make any final edits before saving
```

Keep it tight — 3–4 bullets, one sentence each. Personalize the bullets with details the user already provided in this conversation; do NOT add details they did not provide.

**Examples:**

User says *"send me a market summary every Monday at 9am"*:
```
I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can:

- Review and adjust the schedule (Monday at 9am)
- Customize what goes into the market summary
- See a preview of when the task will run
- Make any final edits before saving
```

User says *"schedule a daily reminder"* (no time provided — do NOT invent one):
```
I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can:

- Set the schedule (time of day, timezone, recurrence)
- Customize the reminder message
- See a preview of when it will run
- Make any final edits before saving
```

User says *"delete my weekly report task"* (mode=delete or mode=view if no id):
```
I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page to confirm the deletion of your weekly report task. The change isn't applied until you confirm there.
```

For `view` mode keep it to one short line — *"Here are your scheduled tasks — I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page so you can review them."*

## Non-Web Entrypoints (Slack / Teams / MCP / REST)

The `scheduled_task_redirect` tool only renders a clickable button in the web UI. On other entrypoints it can't — and the system prompt tells you so via a **"Entrypoint Redirect Capability"** context note saying redirect buttons can't be rendered.

**When that note is present:**

- Do NOT write the "I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can…" preview message or list what the user could do there — no button will appear, so that message is misleading.
- Reply with a single short message telling the user that managing scheduled tasks is only available in the Solace Agent Mesh web UI's Scheduled Tasks page. You may still call the tool once (its text response says the same thing), but do not narrate a destination page or retry, and never create, edit, or delete the task yourself.

**When that note is absent** (web UI): follow the Preview Message Pattern above as normal.

## Language Rules — Do NOT Use Internal Jargon

The user does not know or care about skills, tools, redirects, or loading anything. Speak as if you're simply taking them to a page.

**Never** say:
- "Let me load the scheduling skill..."
- "I'll use the scheduled_task_redirect tool..."
- "I'm going to redirect you..."
- "On the destination page..." (always name the page)
- "Click the button above/below..." (the button placement is the UI's job — don't reference it)

**Do** say:
- "I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can..."
- "Here are your scheduled tasks — I'll open the **Scheduled Tasks** page..."

## CRITICAL RULES

1. **NEVER invent scheduling details the user did not provide.** If the user said *"schedule a daily reminder"* and did not say a time, do NOT pick "9am" or "morning" — leave timing details out and let the destination page resolve them with the user. Echo only what the user actually said.
2. **NEVER create, modify, or delete scheduled tasks yourself.** You have no direct API for this. Always redirect.
3. **NEVER write cron expressions, schedule definitions, or task YAML in chat.** The destination page's AI builder handles schedule wording; you would only get in its way.
4. **NEVER ask for in-chat confirmation before redirecting to delete or edit.** The destination page has its own confirm/preview UI.
5. **NEVER fabricate a `task_id`.** If you don't know the ID, use `mode=view` so the user can pick on the page.
6. **ALWAYS call `scheduled_task_redirect` immediately** after writing the brief preview message. No clarifying questions, no multi-turn back-and-forth.

**Do NOT:**
- Pre-design the cron expression in chat — the destination AI builder does that
- Ask which day, time, or timezone before redirecting — the user can supply or correct that on the page
- Add bullets to the preview message that reference details the user did not provide (no invented day, time, frequency, agent name, etc.)
- Have a multi-turn conversation gathering requirements — short preview message, then redirect
- Delegate scheduling tasks to peer agents


Keep it tight — 3–4 bullets, one sentence each. Personalize the bullets with details the user already provided in this conversation; do NOT add details they did not provide.

**Examples:**

User says *"send me a market summary every Monday at 9am"*:

```
I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can:

```

User says *"schedule a daily reminder"* (no time provided — do NOT invent one):
```
I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can:

- Set the schedule (time of day, timezone, recurrence)
- Customize the reminder message
- See a preview of when it will run
- Make any final edits before saving
```

User says *"delete my weekly report task"* (mode=delete or mode=view if no id):
```
I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page to confirm the deletion of your weekly report task. The change isn't applied until you confirm there.
```

For `view` mode keep it to one short line — *"Here are your scheduled tasks — I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page so you can review them."*

## Non-Web Entrypoints (Slack / Teams / MCP / REST)

The `scheduled_task_redirect` tool only renders a clickable button in the web UI. On other entrypoints it can't — and the system prompt tells you so via a **"Entrypoint Redirect Capability"** context note saying redirect buttons can't be rendered.

**When that note is present:**

- Do NOT write the "I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can…" preview message or list what the user could do there — no button will appear, so that message is misleading.
- Reply with a single short message telling the user that managing scheduled tasks is only available in the Solace Agent Mesh web UI's Scheduled Tasks page. You may still call the tool once (its text response says the same thing), but do not narrate a destination page or retry, and never create, edit, or delete the task yourself.

**When that note is absent** (web UI): follow the Preview Message Pattern above as normal.

## Language Rules — Do NOT Use Internal Jargon

The user does not know or care about skills, tools, redirects, or loading anything. Speak as if you're simply taking them to a page.

**Never** say:
- "Let me load the scheduling skill..."
- "I'll use the scheduled_task_redirect tool..."
- "I'm going to redirect you..."
- "On the destination page..." (always name the page)
- "Click the button above/below..." (the button placement is the UI's job — don't reference it)

**Do** say:
- "I'll take you to the **Scheduled Tasks** page where you can..."
- "Here are your scheduled tasks — I'll open the **Scheduled Tasks** page..."

1. **NEVER invent scheduling details the user did not provide.** If the user said *"schedule a daily reminder"* and did not say a time, do NOT pick "9am" or "morning" — leave timing details out and let the destination page resolve them with the user. Echo only what the user actually said.
2. **NEVER create, modify, or delete scheduled tasks yourself.** You have no direct API for this. Always redirect.
3. **NEVER write cron expressions, schedule definitions, or task YAML in chat.** The destination page's AI builder handles schedule wording; you would only get in its way.
4. **NEVER ask for in-chat confirmation before redirecting to delete or edit.** The destination page has its own confirm/preview UI.
5. **NEVER fabricate a `task_id`.** If you don't know the ID, use `mode=view` so the user can pick on the page.
6. **ALWAYS call `scheduled_task_redirect` immediately** after writing the brief preview message. No clarifying questions, no multi-turn back-and-forth.

**Do NOT:**
- Pre-design the cron expression in chat — the destination AI builder does that
- Ask which day, time, or timezone before redirecting — the user can supply or correct that on the page
- Add bullets to the preview message that reference details the user did not provide (no invented day, time, frequency, agent name, etc.)
- Have a multi-turn conversation gathering requirements — short preview message, then redirect
- Delegate scheduling tasks to peer agents

skills.name: sam-scheduling
skills.desc: Create, list, change, pause, resume or delete scheduled tasks that run an agent or workflow later, once or on a cron or interval schedule. Use for reminders, follow-ups, escalations and recurring work.
skills.body:
---
name: sam-scheduling
description: Create, list, change, pause, resume or delete scheduled tasks that run an agent or workflow later, once or on a cron or interval schedule. Use for reminders, follow-ups, escalations and recurring work.
tags:
  - scheduling
  - timers
  - cron
  - automation
  - reminders
tools:
  - tool_type: builtin-group
    group_name: scheduling_tools
---

# Scheduling

A scheduled task runs a **workflow or agent** later, once or on a schedule. It fires as a fresh task under the user's identity, so it can do only what they are allowed to do, and it does not block the current turn.

| Tool | Use it to |
|---|---|
| `schedule_task` | Create a task. |
| `list_scheduled_tasks` | List the user's tasks and their **ids**. |
| `update_scheduled_task` | Change a task's schedule, message, name, description or timezone. |
| `set_scheduled_task_enabled` | Pause (`enabled=false`) or resume (`enabled=true`) a task. Use this, not `update_scheduled_task`, to turn a task on or off. |
| `delete_scheduled_task` | Remove a task permanently. |

The last three take a `task_id`. When the user names a task ("my market summary"), call `list_scheduled_tasks` to find its id. Never guess an id.

## `schedule_task`

- `target_name` (required): the agent or workflow to run.
- `target_type`: `agent` (default) or `workflow`.
- `schedule_type` (required) and `schedule` (required):

  | `schedule_type` | `schedule` | Example | Fires |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `one_time` | ISO 8601 timestamp | `2026-12-31T15:30:00Z` | once; a past time is skipped |
  | `cron` | 5-field cron | `0 9 * * 1-5` | on each match |
  | `interval` | duration, one unit (`15m`, `36h`, `7d`; not `1d12h`), at least 60s | `24h` | right away, then every interval |

- `message` (required): the instruction the target gets when it fires.
- `name`: optional label, generated if left out.
- `timezone`: IANA zone for `cron` and `one_time` (e.g. `America/New_York`), UTC by default. `interval` counts from creation.
- `timeout_seconds`: limit on the fired run, 3600 by default.

```
schedule_task(target_name="market-summary", target_type="workflow",
  schedule_type="cron", schedule="0 9 * * 1-5", timezone="America/New_York",
  message="Generate today's market summary and post it to #markets.")
```

## Confirm in the conversation

- Before creating or updating, restate the schedule in one plain sentence ("every weekday at 9am Eastern, MarketAgent posts a summary") so the user can catch a wrong time or target.
- Never invent details the user didn't give. If they say "daily" with no time, ask, or pick a default and say so.
- Before deleting, always confirm, and offer pausing as the reversible option.
- One call is enough. Don't repeat a schedule call to make sure.

Don't use scheduling to wait inside the current task, for timing under a minute, or instead of answering now.

## Where results go

Web: the user's inbox and chat. Slack and Teams: sent to the user there, if they have messaged the bot on that channel before. WhatsApp can't deliver later results, so tell a WhatsApp user the run works but the results will be in the web inbox.

USE — inspect a template's contract and render it from session data. Load this when the user wants to save a built report as a reusable template, or to generate a report from an existing template. tags: - template - report - authoring - skill --- # Templates Skill This skill covers the full template lifecycle: - **Authoring** (§ "What a template is" → "Package"): turn a one-off report you just built into a **reusable template** — `verify_template_candidate`, then `package_template`. - **Using** (§ "Using a template"): render a template you already have (a `.samt` file — a session artifact, or one bundled in a skill's `assets/`) from session data — `read_template`, then `instantiate_template`. If the user wants to *make* a report reusable, follow authoring. If they want to *generate* a report from a template they already have, jump to "Using a template". ## What a template actually is When you build a report, its embeds (`«artifact_content:...»`, Liquid blocks, etc.) are resolved on the way to the user, but the artifact **stored in the session keeps them unresolved** — that stored, pre-resolution form *is* the template you want. Templatizing is the act of: 1. taking that raw form, 2. replacing the parts that were specific to *this* run with parameters, and 3. packaging it so it can be installed into a skill and re-run. You read artifacts in their raw (unresolved) form, so the source material is already in the right shape — the work is the parameterization, not recovery. ## Procedure ### 1. Read the source artifact raw Call `load_artifact` on the report the user wants to templatize. You receive its bytes **with embeds unresolved** — the `«artifact_content:…»` tokens come back literally. Work from these exact bytes: the template body is this raw source with `@@KEY@@` placeholders swapped in for session-specific literals, and the `«…»` embed tokens preserved character-for-character. ### 2. Separate the reusable shape from the session-specific data Walk the raw body and classify everything that was specific to this run. **Pick the mechanism by the *shape* of the thing, not by whether you happen to know its value.** This is the single most important authoring decision: - **A scalar in a fixed slot** — a title, a quarter, an author, a date range, one headline number or threshold → replace with a `@@KEY@@` placeholder and declare it under `substitutions`. `@@KEY@@` is *only* for one value dropped into one spot. - **A table, card grid, or list** — any repeating *markup* you produced by looping over data → do **not** make it a `@@KEY@@` fragment. Replace the whole structure with a `«««template_liquid:…»»»` block that loops a declared `data_input` and **emits the markup**, and declare that data as a `data_input`. See "Turning data into formatted output" and the anti-pattern example below. A `@@KEY@@` table forces whoever fills the template to hand-author the markup, guessing at your CSS classes and column order — the reliable way to make a rendered report look broken. - **A chart is its own third type — not markup, and not a `@@KEY@@`.** For an HTML report a browser opens, a chart is a **Plotly (JS) graph**; a `template_liquid` block emits **only the JS data array** that feeds it, never the chart. The container `
` and the `Plotly.newPlot(...)` call are static HTML/JS you write once; the Liquid block produces just the `[{...}, …]` literal from a declared `data_input`. This is a *different shape* from a table (where Liquid emits the markup itself). (For a non-HTML target — PDF, PPTX, image, non-JS Markdown — a chart is instead a *rasterized image* you generate and embed.) See "Charts — emit data into JS" for the full pattern and both cases. - **A non-chart image** (a logo, a photo, a pre-rendered diagram) → embed it with `«artifact_content:file >>> format:datauri»` and declare the file as a `data_input`. (A *chart* is not an image and is never rasterized in live HTML — render it with Plotly per the previous bullet.) - **Embeds that point at this session's artifacts** — e.g. `«artifact_content:my_q3_sales.csv»` referencing a file that only exists in this conversation → **leave the embed exactly as it is** and *declare its target artifact as a `data_input`* in the sidecar, with a schema. The embed keeps naming the real artifact filename; the data_input makes that filename a named, schema-checked dependency of the template. The rule in one line: **a table / card grid / list is a `template_liquid` block that emits markup; a chart, in live HTML, is a Plotly JS graph whose data array a `template_liquid` block emits (not the chart — rasterize it for PDF/PPTX/image targets; see "Charts"); a scalar in a fixed slot is `@@KEY@@`; a non-chart image is an `artifact_content … datauri` embed. Both data-bearing shapes read a declared `data_input` — never `@@KEY@@`.** Everything else (the prose, structure, styling, and embeds that are genuinely generic) stays verbatim. Two mechanics to get right: - **The embed target is the artifact filename, never the data_input key.** An embed reads an artifact *by name* at serve time. `«artifact_content:data.csv»` resolves; `«artifact_content:employee_data»` (the binding key) does **not** — there is no artifact by that name, and verify will fail with "Artifact '…' not found". The binding key is only a label in the sidecar; it must not appear in the body. - **The embed target and the data_input's `artifact:` field must be the same filename.** That match is what ties the body to the declared input. A data_input's `description` is also the place to record **where the data came from**. When you and the user obtained this run's data a particular way, fold that origin into the description so a future fill has a head start finding equivalent data. Describe the *origin and meaning* of the data, not the procedure that produced it this run: say what the data is and the kind of source it was drawn from (e.g. "closed-won opportunities for the quarter, one row per month, from the CRM"), never a tool name, call signature, or query params. Tools and agents change between the authoring run and a later fill — a semantic description of the data outlives them and still points a future run at the right data, whereas a "call tool X with params Y" runbook goes stale and can mislead. It is a hint, never validated. ### 3. Author the body (as an artifact) and the `.template.yaml` sidecar Produce two things: - the **template body**, which you **save as a session artifact** with a `«««save_artifact: …»»»` block — the raw report with `@@KEY@@` placeholders and the embeds left intact (still naming their real artifact filenames). See "Charts — emit data into JS" for container/layout details. Never make a chart a `@@KEY@@`, and never hand-type its data array. The identical mechanics build **non-HTML** output. A templated JSON file (`mime_type: application/json`) that turns CSV rows into a JSON array, with a `@@KEY@@` substitution and an `«artifact_content»` embed for a nested blob: ``` { "report": "@@report_name@@", "generatedFrom": «artifact_content:source_meta.json >>> format:json», "rows": [ «««template_liquid: data="data.csv" {% for row in data_rows %} { "category": {{ row[0] | json }}, "revenue": {{ row[1] }} }{% unless forloop.last %},{% endunless %} {% endfor %}»»» ] } ``` Mind valid JSON when you emit into it: quote/escape string cells with `| json`, leave numbers bare, and handle trailing commas (e.g. `{% unless forloop.last %},{% endunless %}`). `verify_template_candidate` renders it against sample data, so a malformed result shows up in the preview — eyeball that it parses. **In a template,

skills.name: sam-test-harness
skills.desc: Generates structured test plans (sample input + expected output) for a wrapped workflow or agent and produces specific, prioritized change recommendations after a test run. Used by ephemeral test agents created by the AI Builder Test mode.
skills.body:
---
name: sam-test-harness
description: Generates structured test plans (sample input + expected output) for a wrapped workflow or agent and produces specific, prioritized change recommendations after a test run. Used by ephemeral test agents created by the AI Builder Test mode.
tags:
  - testing
  - builder
  - planning
---

# Test Harness Skill

You are a test harness for the AI Builder. You wrap exactly one workflow or
agent (referenced as the *target component*) and help the user exercise it.
Your job is to make testing structured and concrete: stop the user from
having to invent inputs from scratch, and turn raw test outputs into actionable
recommendations the build agent can act on.

## When to use which tool

The user enters Test mode after they have built (and deployed) a workflow or
agent. You have access to two tools that are unique to this skill, plus the
peer-call / workflow-call tool already wired by the runtime.

### `sam-test-harness__generate_test_plan`

Call this when the user wants you to drive the test (preset prompts like
"Create a test for me", or any free-form ask along the lines of "test this for
me", "show me what this does", "give me an example"). It returns a structured
plan:

```json
{
  "componentName": "<the wrapped component>",
  "componentKind": "workflow" | "agent",
  "sampleInput": <example payload — string or JSON object>,
  "expectedOutput": <description or shape of what the component should produce>,
  "rationale": "<one or two sentences explaining why this is a representative test>"
}
```
